uniequip_002_blaze2:
'D-Don't you go dismissing it as crude and simple just yet! There's a story behind it!
'Before I came to Rhodes Island, I moved back near my old home in Victoria for a spell. No one was really taking care of things there, and life was hard for the Infected. Back then, I was busy helping them fight for wages and medicine. I was also worried that my actions might cause my mum trouble. That's why I never went back to see her for years.
'I gave whatever medicine I could get my hands on to people who were sicker than I was. I felt like I could still walk around just fine, that I could hold out for a long time. But one day, without any warning, I just collapsed. My blood felt like it was boiling, my organs felt like porcelain about to crack from the heat...
'I'd imagined that, when I finally fell, I'd be unwilling to accept defeat, unable to let go of the workers I was helping. But when the moment actually came, and I was lying there alone in my shack... all I did was claw around for some scrap wood and carve a crude and tiny wooden lamp. I had no matches, so I lit it with a drop of my own blood, and then I just kept staring at it.
'I remembered how my mum used to light one of those lamps at the front door. Through all those years, we never moved, and she never stopped doing it. She said it was so when my dad finally came back, he could find his way home. Every time I went back home, that lamp was what stuck in my mind the most. And I was more surprised than anyone that, when I was about to die, that lamp was what I wanted to see most, more than anything. Somehow, though I failed to realize it at the time, staring at it eased my pain and dampened my symptoms... I was able to hold on until my companions found me.
'This lamp? No, this isn't that same broken old lamp—I made a new one. I'm no master craftsman, but you're not gonna turn up your nose at my creations, are you?'
When Ning Yin first heard Blaze tell her that story, all she felt was fear at the thought of what Blaze had been through. Next, when she thought about how Blaze had come all this way in the middle of the New Years holiday to bring her that lamp, a gift of such special significance, she forced a smile and praised the gift.
'No, that's not why I'm telling you all this... ah, listen to me, stumbling over my words again!' Blaze let her actions speak instead, hanging the lamp in Ning Yin's tiny apartment. Then she began briskly setting out the food and drink she'd brought. The smell of warm food slowly brought Ning Yin back to herself. It had been far too long since her little apartment had felt this lively. The lamp's soft, hand-crafted glow chased away every trace of loneliness.
'It's not the lamp that matters,' Blaze said quietly, 'but what it reminds you of, right?'
uniequip_003_blaze2:
'"It's nothing"—except something did happen. Maybe the other person really doesn't mind, or maybe they mind a great deal and have chosen not to say so. They might stay quiet because they know you too well and are afraid of hurting your feelings. Or because they don't know you well and don't care to waste breath on you.
'"You decide"—it sounds like they're leaving it up to you, but it can be a show of trust, or it can be indifference and disdain. If it's the former, then in the end you still have to go by the wishes of the person who said it, as a way of showing gratitude and respect. If it's the latter, it gets far more complicated: not only can you not actually decide for yourself, you also have to work out just what you did to offend them in the first place—
'This is such a headache!
'Compared to those people, even the cave musbeasts out in the desert, the ones that cry out only once in their whole lives, come off as chatterboxes!'
Blaze snapped the pen in her hand clean in two, spattering ink all over herself. She let out a long sigh and rummaged through the guest room for ages, only to turn up the one set of Tianshi-style clothes Leizi had prepared for her.
'This is all Lin Qingyan's fault. She didn't warn me in advance, so not only did I make a fool of myself in the street, now I have to write my own cheat sheet just to talk to people!' Recalling those scenes on Baizao's main street a couple of days earlier, Blaze couldn't help but put a hand to her forehead and sigh.
'Next time I see a few people arguing and shoving at a restaurant counter, I am never hauling them off to the Central Judicial Office again!
'Next time a server asks me with a big smile whether my tea has gone flat and would I like a fresh pot, I am never saying "sure" and then sitting there until closing time!
'What's so wrong with just saying what you mean?!' The angrier Blaze got the more she stewed, until she flung the cheat sheet, notebook and all, into the corner of the guest room.
......
Gu Zhuhuang returned to the guest room and gave her luggage one last check. Tomorrow she would be leaving Baizao. A notebook lying in the corner beneath the curtain caught her eye. She picked it up, and remembered what she had been like when she first arrived in Baizao.
'What's so wrong with just saying what you mean...' Gu Zhuhuang gave it some serious thought. 'Turns out there is something.'
She simply dug a pen out of her suitcase and, continuing on from the last line on that little slip of paper, wrote a few lines of reply to the girl she had been.
'Blaze, when you set foot in Yan, this homeland you don't know, you couldn't help feeling worried and afraid. But once you stop being afraid, once you really think of yourself as one of the people here, you'll find that being direct is perfectly fine after all. Frankness and courage are good qualities in Yan too.
'Besides, sometimes the words that never got said are the ones that stay with people the longest.'
